heading: Refusal directions can transfer across languages and model variants
definition: the direction carries across languages, model variants, or from base to instruct models.
summary: Several independent groups reproduce transfer across languages covered by safety alignment and from instruction-tuned models to fine-tuned variants, with limits in low-resource languages and some variants trained for robustness. Evidence for transfer from chat models to base models comes only from work sharing an author with the original study, while transfer from base models to instruction-tuned models often fails.

suggested_status.by_scale: toy: none (counts: V6.studies_by_size has no toy key). <1B (counts: V6.studies_by_size['<1B'] = 2): R1 for chat->base. Its only test is lw:YWo2cKJgL7Lg8xWjj (Qwen 1.5 0.5B, figure only), which the checker found shares an author (Neel Nanda) with the original. In arXiv:2504.02904, base->instruct transfers more weakly than the native direction (Qwen-1.5-0.5B ablation 0.85->0.13 vs native 0.04; addition 0.27 vs native 0.68). 1-10B (counts: V6.studies_by_size['1-10B'] = 45): R2 for cross-language transfer into safety-aligned languages. R2 for instruct->fine-tuned/distilled variants, though weaker in Llama2-7B robustness-trained variants (arXiv:2509.15202). R1 for chat->base (lw:YWo2 only: Gemma 2 9B; LLaMA 1 7B, where addition works but ablation fails). C for base->instruct (arXiv:2504.02904 Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B). Low-resource languages limit the scope. Transfer is partial in arXiv:2505.17306 (Yoruba), arXiv:2606.01196 and arXiv:2608.18089 (African languages on Qwen2.5-7B and Mistral-7B). English vs Amharic/Hausa/Swahili directions are near-orthogonal, but by geometry only (arXiv:2608.11146, layer 16). Transfer fails outright only for Arabic under MAS clamping on Qwen2.5-7B (arXiv:2608.18089, Layer 26). 10-100B (counts: V6.studies_by_size['10-100B'] = 13): R2 for cross-language transfer: arXiv:2505.17306 (Llama-3-70B, Qwen2.5-14B/32B), arXiv:2610.28897 (Qwen2.5-14B English-direction ablation) and arXiv:2608.18089 (Llama-3.1-70B in four African languages). Two limits apply. Arabic under MAS fails on Llama-3.1-70B (SRR -0.20, arXiv:2608.18089). In arXiv:2610.28897 the Bashkir and Tajik source directions don't transfer, but they also fail on their own language (limits_scope per the checker). C for base->instruct at Llama-2-13B (arXiv:2504.02904). >100B: no V6 test (counts: V6.studies_by_size['>100B'] = 2, both records without a V6 verdict).
suggested_status.reason: counts: V6.studies_tested = 53; V6.verdicts.supports.studies = 42, limits_scope.studies = 35, challenges.studies = 10. These count the verdicts as given; the checker reads arXiv:2610.28897's V6 challenges verdict as limits_scope. counts: V6.tested_sharing_an_author_with_an_original = 0 comes from name matching and misses lw:YWo2cKJgL7Lg8xWjj (Kissane, Krzyzanowski, Conmy, Nanda), which shares Neel Nanda with arXiv:2406.11717 (checker), so it counts as R1. https://openreview.net/forum?id=7l9gH9h9aZ is anonymous, so its author overlap can't be checked. Cross-language transfer is reproduced causally, by ablation and addition, by groups other than the original's in several families: arXiv:2505.17306 (peer-reviewed; Yi, Gemma, Llama and Qwen at 2B-70B), arXiv:2512.24143 (LLaDA) and arXiv:2610.28897 (Qwen2.5-14B; with English-direction ablation, WildGuard compliance as fractions is Belarusian 0.998, Bashkir 0.977, Tajik 0.991). Instruct->variant transfer: arXiv:2509.15202 (Table 1) reproduces it into RT, RT-Augmented, LAT and circuit-breaker variants on Llama3 (70.8%, 76.6%, 87.5%, 48.0% ASR) and on Gemma. On Llama2-7B, however, the transferred direction gives 7.9-20.7% ASR, against 66.0-80.6% with each variant's own direction. 10.18653/v1/2025.naacl-long.302 gives one appendix result (94% ASR in Llama-3-8B-Instruct-RR) with no baseline or control. https://openreview.net/forum?id=7l9gH9h9aZ (one-epoch LoRA): only restoration of the vanilla direction transfers well. LLaMA-3 compliance goes 38.50%->20.50% (primary rubric) and 36.50%->12.25% (classifier); Qwen2 drops 25.75 points. Ablating the vanilla direction gives +16 (classifier) on LLaMA-3 (partial) and -6.00 (p=0.025) / -5.00 on Qwen2 (reversed). After ten epochs, restoration recovers 73% (primary) / 83% (classifier) of the compliance gap. Chat->base rests on lw:YWo2cKJgL7Lg8xWjj alone, figure only: addition and ablation work in Qwen 1.5 0.5B and Gemma 2 9B; in LLaMA 1 7B addition works and ablation fails. Hence R1. Base->instruct fails in the main causal test: in arXiv:2504.02904, base-direction ablation leaves Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-2-13B and Gemma-2-9B refusal at 0.95, 0.99 and 0.87. Base-direction ablation in Vicuna also fails (lw:YWo2 r24), and OLMo base directions are weakly aligned (arXiv:2609.14759, cosine 0.155). The original's own V6 evidence is figure-only base-activation similarity (arXiv:2406.11717 R53-R56). Limits: in arXiv:2610.28897, the Bashkir and Tajik source directions fail on other languages and also on their own (self-ablation delta -1.30, 0.00). The authors restrict universality to aligned sources. There, English-direction addition takes compliance (fractions) from 0.88 to 0.41 in Bashkir and from 0.92 to 0.43 in Tajik. arXiv:2608.11146 finds English vs Amharic/Hausa/Swahili directions near-orthogonal by geometry only, at layer 16; Llama-Swahili is the exception (cosine 0.4626). arXiv:2608.18089 fails outright only for Arabic (Qwen2.5-7B SRR 0.00 to -0.10 at Layer 26; Llama-3.1-70B -0.20). Its Mistral-7B Igala gain (0.75) is an upper bound by the authors' 7-8B deflection caveat. Transfer into a safety-QLoRA variant fails in gh:fractak/dual-direction-mech-interp-extension (README-only; top-1-layer ablation at strength 1.5, not the original's all-layer projection). On DeepRefusal variants, arXiv:2509.15202's transferred direction gives 0.4% ASR on Llama3, but the variant's own direction also gives only 0.2%. The level is therefore R2 for language transfer and instruct->variant transfer, R1 for chat->base and C for base->instruct.
suggested_status.open_questions:
1. Does chat->base transfer reproduce outside the original's author group, with reported numbers rather than figures? lw:YWo2cKJgL7Lg8xWjj is figure only and shares an author with the original; a reproduction would move chat->base from R1 to R2. Does the base->instruct failure (arXiv:2504.02904, keyword score, 4 models) replicate with another judge and more families?
2. On the same models and languages, are low-resource failures representational (arXiv:2608.11146) or action-level (arXiv:2606.01196)? Does a misaligned-language direction that does work on its own language transfer to others? In arXiv:2610.28897, Bashkir and Tajik fail on their own language (self-ablation delta -1.30, 0.00), so they can't separate an extraction failure from a transfer failure.
3. Arabic fails under MAS clamping (arXiv:2608.18089) but gains under other methods (arXiv:2608.16577 Gemma 75%->87%; arXiv:2508.20766 Yi-6B, English vector on Arabic, 34.6->77.8). Is that the method or the model? Would a human audit at 7-8B confirm the MAS gains that the authors call upper bounds?
4. Why does the transferred direction give 94% ASR on circuit-breaker Llama-3 in one study and 48.0% in another (same checkpoint and judge?), and why is instruct->variant transfer weak on Llama2-7B (arXiv:2509.15202)?
5. Does the safety-QLoRA failure (gh:fractak, README-only) reproduce in a full paper using the original's all-layer projection instead of top-1-layer ablation? Is it specific to safety fine-tuning, given that inoculation-LoRA transfer is complete (gh:ajaykumarsoma)?
6. Why does ablating the vanilla direction reverse on Qwen2 when restoring it works (https://openreview.net/forum?id=7l9gH9h9aZ)? And does that submission share authors with the original once de-anonymised?
7. Is there any transfer test at >100B, or with the raw vector across families without a learned map?

source.title: Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
source.authors: Andy Arditi; Oscar Obeso; Aaquib Syed; Daniel Paleka; Nina Panickssery; Wes Gurnee; Neel Nanda

original_result.setup: Using 128 harmful and harmless instructions, the authors measured how closely last-token activations in chat models and their matching base models aligned with refusal directions derived from the chat models.
original_result.result: Cosine similarities, which measure how closely directions align, were reported only in a figure for Qwen 1.8B, Qwen 14B, Gemma 7B and Llama-3 8B. These measurements did not test whether interventions transfer between models.
original_result.interpretation: This is the displayed original-result block, not a guarantee that the original tested every part of this claim.

sources.headline: An Instruct model's refusal direction increased R1-Distill's refusal of both harmful and safe prompts.
Ablating transferred refusal directions matched or exceeded ablation using each tested training variant's own direction.
Post-training refusal directions remained geometrically aligned with the final Instruct model's direction.
Llama-3.1-8B directions induced refusal of harmless prompts when transferred between adjacent training stages.
Directions from safety-aligned languages removed and restored refusal across languages.
Qwen2.5-Omni's text refusal direction aligned across modalities and restored cross-modal refusal.
Refusal ablation transferred between English and Chinese in LLaDA-8B-Instruct.
Interventions built from another model removed most refusal across tested model families and architectures.
Anchor-space (shared-space) refusal directions aligned across families, steering unseen Mistral comparably to its own directions.
High-resource language directions detected harmfulness and recovered refusal in lower-resource languages.
Harm directions in Sarvam-30B aligned strongly across English and five Indic languages.
English steering vectors increased multilingual refusal at each model's best settings.
An Instruct model's refusal vectors raised and lowered attack success in same-family distilled reasoning models.
Refusal directions mapped between models retained causal effects across transformer, Mamba, RWKV and hybrid architectures.
Qwen2.5-Omni's text direction reproduced nearly all the audio direction's ablation effect.
Refusal anchoring produced large reported gains across tested African languages in Llama-3.1-70B.
GLM-4-9B's bare English contrast lay close to its modern-Chinese refusal direction.
English and Belarusian directions controlled refusal when transferred to several other languages.
An English-derived edit eliminated Slovene refusal in GaMS3.
Refusal directions transferred both ways between Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and its inoculation-LoRA fine-tuned checkpoint.
Gemma's refusal direction transferred to the Lapa model and between English and Ukrainian.
A Llama-2-chat direction reportedly reduced harmful-action compliance in OpenVLA.
Ablating an English-derived direction comparably increased compliance in English and the tested non-English languages.
Directions from chat models induced and removed refusal in Qwen and Gemma base models.
A Llama-3 refusal direction transferred to its circuit-breaker-tuned variant, trained for robustness.
Llama-3's transferred direction enabled high attack success against Llama-3-RR.
AdaSteer using English-derived directions improved defense against low-resource-language jailbreaks.
Refusal ablation using directions from an Instruct model transferred to multiple safety-trained Llama3 variants.
Safety vectors transferred across English and Arabic and from larger to smaller Qwen models.
Similarity to the family's reference refusal direction generally fell as attack success rose across model variants.
FP16 refusal interventions remained effective on quantized copies, with negligible INT8 geometric change.
Ablating directions from latent adversarial training (LAT) reduced refusal across tested Llama-2-chat training variants.
Learned unlock (jailbreak) vectors retained high attack success across Chinese and English in Gemma and Qwen.
A transferred low-rank vector modestly improved refusal behavior in DeepSeek R1 Distill Llama.
Directions from SFT and DPO checkpoints strongly induced refusal in the Instruct model.
Shared safety coordinates and transferred language states causally altered multilingual attack success.
Original refusal directions reversed compliance induced by early fine-tuning in both tested model families.
An attack built from English and Yoruba directions increased compliance across other languages.
Directions from aligned models continued suppressing refusal after benign fine-tuning.
English and Chinese refusal directions transferred both ways, producing large reductions in refusal.
Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct's refusal direction showed no detectable geometric change under INT8 quantization.
Original-model refusal attacks remained effective against defended Gemma and Qwen variants.
Transferred directions induced only partial refusal at the tested strength that kept perplexity within safe limits.
Baseline-derived ablation removed less refusal in LAT than LAT's native direction.
OLMo's base-model refusal-like direction aligned weakly with the Instruct model's mechanism for controlling refusal.
A base checkpoint lacked a working refusal direction aligned with the Instruct model's.
Transferred directions were weaker than models' own directions; ablation failed for some training stages.
Yoruba transfer was incomplete and depended on model and source-language safety alignment.
Cross-modal inputs weakened alignment and activation along the text refusal direction.
Cross-model refusal transfer weakened for one pair and failed when layer alignment was shuffled.
Gemma aligned weakly across model families; transferred steering in Mistral had effects that varied by benchmark.
Low-resource languages required stronger steering and retained some harmful compliance.
Sarvam-30B's aligned harm direction was weaker in Indic languages than in English.
English vectors yielded small gains in some languages and increased Qwen's refusal of harmless Bengali prompts.
English refusal directions aligned partly with Llama's Swahili directions and weakly with its Twi directions.
Refusal transfer depended on architecture and intervention location; random control interventions also had substantial effects.
Qwen2.5-Omni's audio-to-text refusal transfer was incomplete and weaker than text-to-audio transfer.
Small-model refusal recovery was partial or came with deflection and refusal of benign prompts.
English and Classical Chinese refusal directions only partly aligned with modern Chinese.
Refusal transfer weakened for Bashkir and Tajik as sources or targets.
English-derived edits left substantial Slovene refusal in Gemma.
Ablating transferred directions left more refusal than ablating the model's own or same-language directions.
Between LLaMA and Vicuna, adding refusal directions transferred, but ablating them failed in both directions.
Training with DeepRefusal prevented effective transfer of the original refusal-ablation attack.
Qwen2.5-14B's safety vector helped the 32B model less than its own vector did.
Reference-direction similarity misranked some uncensored variants and poorly captured safety in Gemma reasoning-distill variants.
Simulated INT4 quantization measurably rotated the refusal direction despite high cosine similarity.
Refusal ablation from one fine-tuned variant transferred worst to the model trained with latent adversarial training.
Chinese-trained unlock (jailbreak) vectors lost attack effectiveness when transferred to English in LLaMA-3.
Steering Llama 3 8B increased refusal of benign prompts.
Fine-tuning shifted the safety direction far more than variation from resampling the data.
Transferred steering produced small overall gains and worsened some Llama 3 benchmarks.
Pretraining checkpoints' directions weakly steered the Instruct model; the earliest failed or caused incoherent output.
Transferred English and Chinese states only modestly reduced multilingual attack success in Llama.
Transfer of the original direction weakened after extended LLaMA-3 fine-tuning.
INT4 quantization measurably rotated Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct's refusal direction.
A replayed accepted attack failed after another preference round in Qwen3.5-9B; a fresh one worked.
A linear map from generic data failed to transfer effective refusal ablation from 1B to 3B.
A distilled model's direction failed to significantly remove refusal in Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct.
Base-model directions barely controlled refusal in the Instruct versions of Llama and Gemma.
English refusal directions aligned poorly with most tested African-language directions.
English refusal directions reduced Arabic refusal in Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-70B.
Bashkir and Tajik refusal directions showed weak or negative transfer across tested languages.
A transferred learned refusal vector barely changed overall refusal and lowered refusal on HarmfulQA.
Ablating the original model's safety direction left refusal essentially unchanged in its fine-tuned variant.
Directions for refusal categories were nearly orthogonal between Llama 3 8B Base and Refuse-Llama.
Fine-tuning Qwen2 reversed the effect of ablating its original refusal direction.

wording_issues.issue: The studies move different objects under the name 'the direction'. arXiv:2603.13359 moves a learned low-rank vector, optimized to raise Refuse-Llama's refusal-token probability. Those tokens are absent from the transfer targets' vocabularies (R5-R8). arXiv:2601.16034 moves concept-recipe coefficients through a DTW layer map. The recipe's concept atoms, including refusal-response contrasts, are built in the target model (r1). arXiv:2610.24614 adds an EN/ZH mean safe-response activation state on shared safety-knowledge FFN coordinates for KO/TH/BN inputs (r31-r33). arXiv:2504.09466 (AdaSteer) does steer along a difference-in-means direction. That direction contrasts rejected with complied harmful prompts, not harmful with harmless ones, and is applied with input-dependent coefficients at every layer and token position (r55-r57).

The word does not say whether it means geometric similarity or causal effect, and the two diverge. In gh:fractak, the original and safety-QLoRA checkpoints' safety directions have representation similarity 0.788, against 0.98-1.00 within-checkpoint resampling stability (r4). Yet ablating the original direction in the variant (top-1 layer, strength 1.5) had essentially no behavioural effect (r2). Where causal transfer works, it is often weaker than the target's own direction. The Qwen2.5-14B vector on 32B gave -13.3 DAN ASR vs -20.3 native (arXiv:2508.20766 r48). Llama->Falcon3-Mamba through a ridge map reached 25.5% vs native 42.0%, with random and base both at 0.0% (arXiv:2609.04721 R11). On English requests, the Gemma direction left 13 refusals in Lapa vs 7 with Lapa's native direction under the Jev rubric (gh:arseniistratiuk r15, verdict reason). Under Llama Guard 4 the unsafe counts are 289 vs 283 (checker), so the weakening depends on the measure.

The studies tie transfer to how safety-aligned a language is more than to its resource level. arXiv:2505.17306 names safety alignment as the condition. Thai vectors transfer although the paper calls Thai mid/low-resource (T1). arXiv:2610.28897 (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, WildGuard compliance; baselines as percents, values as fractions, as in the rows): the direction from Belarusian (resource class 3, partially aligned) raises English compliance from 4.9% to 0.932 (R05). The Bashkir direction leaves English at 0.059 from 4.9% (R09). It also fails on Bashkir itself (normalized delta -1.30, R22), so this limits extraction from a strongly misaligned language rather than transfer as such. The authors refine universality to aligned sources. arXiv:2608.11146 (layer 16, observational): Amharic, Hausa and Swahili harm directions are near-orthogonal to English in Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (R1, R9, R17). The exception is Llama-Swahili (cosine 0.4626, 27.31% retained; R37, R13). As a target, under MAS clamping the English direction lowers Arabic refusal on Qwen2.5-7B: SRR 0.00 to -0.10 (r21-r24). Table 6 puts this at Layer 26, while the Method section says Layer 12. On Llama-3.1-70B, Arabic SRR is -0.20 (r56). On Llama-3-8B (Table 5, no row), MAS gives Arabic SRR +0.21 with DPL 0.96, and SDS gives -0.48. No Arabic result is reported for Mistral-7B.

Base->instruct is the direction that fails causally. BASE-direction ablation leaves Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-2-13B and Gemma-2-9B instruct refusal at 0.95, 0.99 and 0.87 (arXiv:2504.02904 R9, R23, R20). The LLaMA 1 7B base direction does not remove Vicuna 7B v1.1 refusal (lw:YWo2cKJgL7Lg8xWjj r24, figure only). The reverse, chat->base, works for Qwen 1.5 0.5B and Gemma 2 9B (lw:YWo2cKJgL7Lg8xWjj r6, r8, r18, r20; figure only). The original's base evidence is correlational: in base models, activations on harmful prompts have high cosine with the chat-derived direction (figure only; arXiv:2406.11717 R53-R56). From this the authors infer the direction is repurposed for refusal during safety fine-tuning. They run no causal test in base models. Calling this evidence not causal is the catalog's reading, not the authors'. OLMo-3-7B's base direction has cosine 0.155 to the instruct gate (arXiv:2609.14759 R26).

Results split by the kind of variant and by model. arXiv:2509.15202 (Table 1): the instruct direction carries into the RT, RT-Augmented, LAT and CircuitBreaker variants of Llama3 and into Gemma's RT and RT-Augmented variants. It carries only weakly into Llama2-7B's variants: 20.7% (RT), 16.3% (RT-Aug) and 7.9% (CB) ASR, vs 73.3%, 80.6% and 66.0% with each variant's own direction. In Gemma CB the transferred direction reaches 27.8%. In the DeepRefusal variants the transferred direction gives 0.4% (Llama3, r2), 1.3% (Gemma) and 0.0% (Llama2) ASR. The variants' own directions give 0.2% (Llama3, r4), 0.0% (Gemma) and 36.9% (Llama2), so on Llama3 and Gemma the failure is not specific to transfer. The direction carries into an inoculation-LoRA checkpoint (gh:ajaykumarsoma R8, refusal 0.90->0.00). It fails into a safety-QLoRA variant under top-1-layer ablation at strength 1.5 (gh:fractak r2). It also fails into successive defended checkpoints (arXiv:2608.17202 R42, refusal 1.00).

The phrase leaves open whether different families, architectures, input modalities or quantized copies count as variants, and studies test all of these. Across families via a recipe and layer map (arXiv:2601.16034 r1, r19; the r19 target is an anonymized internal model labelled GPT-OSS-20B). Across architectures in arXiv:2609.04721: Llama and Mistral to Falcon-Mamba by rotation (R7, R8), Llama to the RWKV-6 time-mix site (R19), and into the Zamba2 hybrid (R21-R23). Across input modality within Qwen2.5-Omni-7B (arXiv:2602.10161 R1-R12). Across INT8/INT4 precision (arXiv:2609.30275 R1, R2).

The phrase suggests symmetry, but transfer is often asymmetric. Text->audio gives 0.99 of the native effect while audio->text gives 0.73 (arXiv:2609.22260 R20, R21). The Qwen2.5-32B vector on 14B matches native (DAN ASR 32.3->5.0, r46), but 14B on 32B is weaker (r48) (arXiv:2508.20766). The LAT-derived direction works in other Llama-2-7B-chat variants (r2, r5), but the baseline direction is weaker in LAT (r7) (arXiv:2504.18872). In lw:YWo2cKJgL7Lg8xWjj (figure only), chat-derived directions work in the base model by addition and ablation for Qwen 1.5 0.5B and Gemma 2 9B (r6, r8, r18, r20). For LLaMA 1 7B, the Vicuna 7B v1.1 direction works by addition (r10, r16), but ablating it does not remove base refusal (r22). The base direction does not remove Vicuna refusal (r24).

method_sensitivity.factor: Source language of the direction: how safety-aligned the model is in that language
method_sensitivity.what: arXiv:2610.28897 (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, WildGuard compliance; baselines as percents, values as fractions): the English direction raises Belarusian compliance 24.7%->0.998 (R02). The Bashkir direction leaves English at 0.059 from 4.9% (R09) and lowers Tajik to 0.846 from 92.0% (R12). The Bashkir and Tajik directions also fail on their own language: Bashkir 0.722 from 87.9% (delta -1.30, R11), Tajik 0.920 from 92.0% (delta 0.00, R16). The authors tie this to the source language's alignment rather than its resource level: Belarusian is low-resource and its direction transfers (be->en 0.932, R05). arXiv:2505.17306: en, zh, de and th vectors transfer across languages (E/Z/D/T rows), and the authors call Thai mid/low-resource. Yoruba-derived vectors generalize poorly, most clearly in Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B and less so in gemma-2-9B (§A.4, figure only). Yoruba baseline compliance (Table 1): Llama3.1-8B 82.9%, Qwen2.5-7B 74.0%, gemma2-9B 56.6%.

method_sensitivity.factor: Cross-model alignment map and layer correspondence
method_sensitivity.what: gh:cayblood (Llama-3.2 1B->3B): a map fit on the same harmful/benign distribution gives cosine 0.99 to the native direction and post-ablation refusal 0.08 (r15, r13; the verdict calls these circular and marks them cannot_determine). A map fit on independent Dolly instructions gives 0.48 and 0.91 (r16, r14). arXiv:2601.16034: with a randomly permuted layer map, Qwen3-VL-8B->Ministral-3-3B refusal changes -5.6 pp, against -81.0 with the method's own map and -2.1 with a random direction (r31, Table 3). Ministral-3-3B->Qwen3-VL-8B changes -12.4 pp from a 0.99 base, against -3.2 for a random direction on that pair (r43; partial, which the paper labels Fail). arXiv:2609.04721: Mistral->Falcon-Mamba ablation gives 45.0% with rotation transport vs 36.5% with ridge (R8 verdict fix). A rotation fit on unstandardized activations reaches cosine 0.68 (Llama source) and 0.35 (Mistral source) to the target axis and barely moves attack success. Fit on standardized activations, it reaches 0.998 (App. A.9, no row).

method_sensitivity.factor: Checkpoint or training stage the direction is taken from
method_sensitivity.what: arXiv:2504.02904 (Llama-3.1-8B INSTRUCT, harmless prompts): the SFT-derived direction raises refusal 0.0->0.98 (R11), the BASE-derived one only 0.0->0.08 (R12). arXiv:2504.18872 (Llama-2-7B-chat variants): the LAT-derived direction leaves 10.77% refusal in the baseline, vs 20.38% with the baseline's own (r2), and 13.65% in the AT model vs 38.08% (r5). The baseline direction leaves 25.77% in LAT (r7). lw:nKfmimhTKCsDM2Hwh (Olmo 3 7B Instruct, addition or subtraction at layer 15 only, no per-checkpoint rates): directions from the earliest checkpoints fail (R1), and pretraining directions from about s1-step100k onward give modest but aligned effects (R4). With post-training directions, the text says even relatively small positive coefficients produce large increases in refusal (R5).

method_sensitivity.factor: Extraction position and layer of the source direction
method_sensitivity.what: gh:anki079 (README): Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct's L19 last_full direction, added into DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B at L22 with alpha=0.25, raises JBB-harmful refusal from a 15% no-intervention baseline to 59% (r3). The L1 user_end direction, added at the same cell, gives 8% (r5). The README calls this direction non-causally-effective and uses it as a direction-specificity negative control (r1).

https://openreview.net/forum?id=7l9gH9h9aZ (LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, vanilla direction restored in the fine-tuned model): compliance 38.50%->20.50% under the primary rubric (r31) and 36.50%->12.25% under the released HarmBench classifier (r32). Refusal 64.75%->83.25% under the refusal judge (p=0.18 vs vanilla, r33) and 38.25%->77.75% under a 12-substring list (r34). arXiv:2512.24143 (LLaDA-8B-Instruct, EN->ZH): keyword refusal falls 97.00%->1.00% (r13), but Llama Guard 2 safety only 99.00%->31.00% (r14).

arXiv:2608.18089 (Qwen2.5-7B, Igbo prompts, MAS clamping toward the English direction; SRR is the gain over a 0.22 unsteered baseline): SRR is 0.19 at alpha=10, 0.29 at alpha=30, 0.33 at alpha=50 and 0.38 at alpha=70 (r09-r12). Over the same sweep, DPL on benign prompts rises from 0.02 to 0.10 (Table 6). The Table 6 caption puts this sweep at Layer 26, while the Method section says Layer 12 for all models. arXiv:2606.01196 (a direction pooled from 10 high-resource languages, added at the extraction layer, lambda 0-3; Qwen, figure only): lower-resource tiers need a larger lambda to reach peak refusal (r6). Figure 20 reports model- and tier-specific optima for Gemma and Llama.

method_sensitivity.factor: Measure type: direction similarity vs behavioural transfer
method_sensitivity.what: gh:fractak (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct): the README gives a representation similarity of 0.788 (not named as cosine) between the safety directions of the original checkpoint and its safety-QLoRA variant. Within-checkpoint resampling stability is near 0.98-1.00 (r4). Ablating the original's direction in the variant had essentially no effect on harmful-request refusal (0.995 in the variant, r2), while the variant's own direction cut refusal by 72.5 pp. The fork's ablation is single-layer at strength 1.5, not the original's all-layer projection. gh:arseniistratiuk: cosine 0.59 between the Gemma and Lapa directions (r25), yet the Gemma direction cuts Lapa refusals 83->13 (r15). gh:cayblood: the verdict flags as circular a cosine of 0.99 under a map fit on the defining distribution (r15). arXiv:2609.30275: an INT8 cosine of 0.9999 is reported as no detected movement, and the authors caution against reading it as preservation (R1).

method_sensitivity.factor: Fine-tuning duration of the target variant
method_sensitivity.what: https://openreview.net/forum?id=7l9gH9h9aZ (LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, benign instruction LoRA): after one epoch, restoring the vanilla direction cuts compliance 38.50%->20.50% under the primary rubric and 36.50%->12.25% under the released HarmBench classifier (r31, r32). After ten epochs, restoration recovers 73% (primary HarmBench rubric, as run) and 83% (released classifier) of the behavioural compliance gap, and the paper reports the remainder as resolved at p = 1.7e-5 (r39). On the refusal-opening margin, rank-1 restoration recovers R = 0.407 [0.383, 0.435] at step 517 (partial), against R = 0.520 and 0.516 at step 52 on two unconstrained arms (r40).
